planting.note: Do not attempt to move plants from the wild — this species is protected or of conservation concern across much of its range, and wild-dug corms almost never survive transplant. There is no reliable commercial source; if a nursery-propagated, lab-grown plant is ever legitimately offered, site it beneath undisturbed conifers in cool, mossy, humus-rich duff with its native soil and fungal partners intact.

directions: This record exists mainly for identification and honest documentation: the fairy slipper is one of the most photographed native orchids in North America and one of the least cultivable, depending on an intact, undisturbed relationship with specific forest fungi that cannot be reproduced in a garden bed or pot. A single pleated basal leaf appears in fall and persists through winter, then a solitary, nodding pink-to-magenta flower with a yellow-bearded pouch opens on a short stem in spring before the plant goes dormant for summer. Never dig or purchase wild-collected plants — most populations decline for years after any digging nearby, even if the plant itself is left undisturbed. Admire and photograph it in its native cool, mossy conifer forest rather than attempting to bring it home.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated corms, never wild-collected stock, directly into living, undisturbed sphagnum moss over saturated, strongly acidic (pH 3.5–5.0) peat in a true bog garden; success even with correctly sourced plants is inconsistent and depends on maintaining the exact wet, nutrient-poor hydrology of a natural bog.

directions: Dragon's mouth is the showiest and most difficult of the classic northeastern bog-orchid trio that also includes grass pink and rose pogonia, bearing a single, brilliant magenta-pink flower with a white, purple-streaked, bearded lip on a slender stem, followed by a solitary grass-like leaf that emerges only after bloom. It depends on a narrower and more specific mycorrhizal fungal partnership than its bog-orchid relatives, and even correctly sourced, nursery-propagated corms planted into an established sphagnum bog frequently fail to persist for more than a few seasons. Only ever purchase symbiotically lab-propagated plants from a specialist native orchid nursery, never wild-collected corms, and expect this to remain a challenge project for an experienced bog gardener rather than a dependable garden perennial. Native populations are declining across its range from wetland drainage, so wild plants should never be disturbed or collected.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society (Native Plant Trust)

planting.note: Only plant nursery-propagated divisions from a specialist Cypripedium propagator, never wild-collected rhizomes; site in cool, moist, humus-rich soil over limestone or other calcareous substrate in the dappled shade of cedar, spruce, or mixed conifer-hardwood forest, mimicking the cold, mossy woodland it needs to persist.

directions: The smallest and rarest of the North American lady's slippers, ram's-head produces a tiny, conical, white pouch veined in pink-purple with hairy, pointed sepals that together give the flower its ram's-head profile, held above a short stem with a few pleated leaves in May and June. It is confined in the wild to cool, calcareous conifer swamps and thin-soiled limestone woodlands, and it is exceptionally intolerant of transplanting or soil disturbance even compared to other native Cypripedium species. A small number of specialist propagators have produced lab-grown plants from seed, and only these should ever be purchased; digging from the wild is both illegal in most of its range and essentially always fatal to the plant. Treat any successfully established planting as a long-term, uncertain project rather than a reliable garden perennial.
